questions.question: A projectile is launched at a speed of $32.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $62^\circ$ above the horizontal. Calculate the magnitude of the initial vertical and horizontal components of the velocity of the projectile.
options: Horizontal $15.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, vertical $29.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
Horizontal $29.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, vertical $15.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
Horizontal $22.1\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, vertical $24.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
Horizontal $24.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, vertical $22.1\ \text{m s}^{-1}$

questions.question: Which combination of quarks makes up a proton?
questions.answer: A proton has charge $+1$: $u+u+d=\frac23+\frac23-\frac13=+1$ (A). ($udd$ is a neutron.)
options: $uud$
$\bar u\bar u\bar d$
$uu\bar d$
$udd$

questions.question: A person on Earth watches a spacecraft fly past Earth at a speed of $0.85c$. An event on the spacecraft takes 43 minutes to occur as measured by the person on the spacecraft. How long does the event take for the observer on Earth?
options: 23 minutes
82 minutes
111 minutes
155 minutes

questions.question: The diagram shows the splitting of the four fundamental forces at the beginning of the universe. Formation of particles, nuclei, atoms and stars could not occur until specific forces existed. Gravity causes particles to attract to each other. Which other forces were required to form the following types of matter?
questions.answer: Atoms need the electromagnetic force to bind electrons to the nucleus (and the strong force to hold the nucleus together), so (D). Protons are not held together by the weak force, so C is wrong.
options: Atoms: strong nuclear and weak nuclear forces.
Nuclei: strong nuclear and electromagnetic forces.
Protons: strong nuclear and weak nuclear forces.
Atoms: strong nuclear and electromagnetic forces.

questions.question: The image shows an experiment that helped to understand the structure of the atom. Who performed this experiment and what was the discovery made?
questions.answer: Alpha particles from a source strike beryllium, producing neutral radiation that knocks protons out of paraffin wax: Chadwick's discovery of the neutron (D).
options: Rutherford: discovery of the neutron
Rutherford: discovery of the nucleus
Chadwick: discovery of the proton
Chadwick: discovery of the neutron

questions.question: The graph shows how the mass of radon-211 in a sample changes over time. Determine the radioactive decay constant for Rn-211.
questions.answer: The mass halves from 12 g to 6 g in about 14.5 h, so $t_{1/2}\approx14.5\times3600=5.2\times10^{4}$ s. $\lambda=\dfrac{\ln2}{t_{1/2}}=\dfrac{0.693}{5.2\times10^{4}}=1.3\times10^{-5}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ (B).

questions.question: The diagram shows the laminated iron core of a transformer. What is the purpose of the laminations in the iron core?
questions.answer: The thin insulated layers limit the size of the eddy current loops in the core, which reduces resistive heating and power loss (B). They reduce, but do not completely prevent, eddy currents (so D is wrong).
options: To make the iron core lighter.
To reduce power loss in the transformer.
To transfer the flux from the primary to the secondary coil.
To prevent the formation of any eddy currents in the iron core.

questions.question: A fan has three points marked on it, X, Y and Z, as shown. As the fan blade spins, the angular speed and linear speed of points X, Y and Z are measured. Rank the angular and linear speed of points X to Z.
questions.answer: All points on a rigid rotating body have the same angular speed $\omega$. Linear speed $v=r\omega$ increases with distance from the axis, and Z is furthest, so $v$ increases from X to Z (B).
options: Angular speed and linear speed both increase from X to Z.
Angular speed is constant, linear speed increases from X to Z.
Angular speed is constant, linear speed increases from Z to X.
Linear speed is constant, angular speed increases from X to Z.

questions.question: Two parallel wires of length 3.5 m carry the same magnitude of current. The two wires are fixed in place, 5.3 cm apart and have a repulsive force of $3.78\times10^{-6}$ N between them. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the current in the wires.
questions.answer: $\dfrac Fl=\dfrac{\mu_0I^2}{2\pi r}$, so $I^2=\dfrac{2\pi rF}{\mu_0l}=\dfrac{2\pi(0.053)(3.78\times10^{-6})}{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(3.5)}=0.286$ and $I=0.535$ A. Parallel wires repel when the currents are in opposite directions (D).
options: 0.286 A in the same direction
0.286 A in the opposite direction
0.535 A in the same direction
0.535 A in the opposite direction

questions.question: The diagram shows a fission reactor. What is the role of the moderator and control rods in a controlled nuclear fission reaction?
questions.answer: The moderator slows fast neutrons by collisions so they are more likely to cause further fission. Control rods absorb neutrons and can be raised or lowered to control the rate of the chain reaction (A).
options: Moderator: a substance that slows neutrons via collision. Control rods: moveable rods that absorb neutrons.
Moderator: a substance that slows neutrons via collision. Control rods: moveable rods that slow neutrons through collision.
Moderator: a substance that absorbs and releases neutrons. Control rods: moveable rods that absorb neutrons.
Moderator: a substance that absorbs neutrons via collision. Control rods: moveable rods that slow neutrons through collision.

questions.question: The diagram shows a metal disc that is free to rotate about the central pole and is not in contact with the magnet. When the metal disc is spun and the magnet is not present, the disc takes approximately 45 seconds to come to a stop. When the metal disc is spun at the same initial rate and the magnet is present, it comes to a stop in approximately 10 seconds. What is the reason for the difference in stopping times?
questions.answer: The part of the disc moving through the magnet's field has a changing flux, so by Faraday's law an emf and eddy currents are induced in the disc. By Lenz's law the magnetic fields of these currents oppose the change (the motion), so the disc slows quickly (D). The disc is not in contact with the magnet, so friction is not involved.
options: Friction between the magnet and disc creates a resistive force that opposes the spinning motion.
Eddy currents form in the disc due to Lenz's law, resulting in magnetic fields that oppose the spinning motion.
Eddy currents form in the magnet due to Faraday's law, resulting in magnetic fields that oppose the spinning motion.
Eddy currents form in the disc due to Faraday's Law, resulting in magnetic fields that oppose the spinning motion.

questions.question: Muons form in the upper atmosphere through nuclear reactions and provide evidence of special relativity. Non-relativistic data about muons: distance from formation to Earth's surface 10 km; half-life of muon 2.2 µs; number of muons reaching Earth 0. What is the reason that relativistic data measured about muons differs from the non-relativistic data?
questions.answer: In the Earth's frame the muons' clocks run slow, so humans observe a longer half-life (time dilation). In the muon's own frame its half-life is unchanged but the distance to the surface is length-contracted. So (B).
options: The muons experience a longer half-life due to time dilation. Humans observe muons travelling a shorter distance to the Earth's surface.
Humans observe muons having a longer half-life due to time dilation. The muons experience length contraction of the distance to Earth's surface.
The muons experience a longer half-life due to time dilation. The muons experience length contraction of the distance to the Earth's surface.
Humans observe muons having a longer half-life due to time dilation. Humans observe muons experiencing length contraction of the distance to Earth's surface.

questions.question: The diagram shows examples of a fission reaction and a fusion reaction. Which of the following is true when comparing the two reactions?
questions.answer: In both reactions the products have less mass than the reactants (mass defect), and the lost mass is released as energy ($E=mc^2$) (B). Both also need an initial input (neutron absorption or high temperature and pressure), and A and D are false.
options: Only fusion reactions require energy to start the reaction.
Both fission and fusion reactions have a net release of energy.
Fission reactions have a net release of energy, fusion reactions have a net absorption of energy.
In fission the products have greater mass than reactants, in fusion the reactants have greater mass than the products.

questions.question: The gold foil experiment is shown. In experiments like this, specific observations are used to make a conclusion about the structure. Which of the following observations matches the conclusion?
questions.answer: The few alpha particles deflected through large angles were repelled by a small, dense, positively charged nucleus (C). Most passing straight through shows the atom is mostly empty space, so A and B pair observations and conclusions the wrong way round. Alpha particles are deflected, not refracted (D).
options: Observation: the majority of alpha particles passed through undeflected. Conclusion: the nucleus was in the centre of the atom.
Observation: a small proportion of particles were deflected or reflected. Conclusion: the atom is mostly empty space.
Observation: a small proportion of alpha particles changed course and were deflected. Conclusion: the nucleus had a positive charge causing deflection of alpha particles.
Observation: a small proportion of particles were deflected or refracted. Conclusion: the nucleus had a positive charge causing deflection of alpha particles.

questions.question: The diagram shows Millikan's oil drop experiment where negatively charged oil droplets fall into a uniform electric field directed downwards. The plates are a distance $d$ apart with potential difference $V$. The oil droplets in the electric field are accelerating downwards. Which of the following is the correct relationship to find the charge $q$ on an oil drop that is accelerating downwards?
questions.answer: A negative drop in a downward field feels an upward electric force $qE=\dfrac{qV}{d}$. If it accelerates downwards, the weight exceeds this: $mg>\dfrac{qV}{d}$, so $q<\dfrac{dmg}{V}$ (A). ($q=dmg/V$ would hold if the drop was stationary.)
options: $q<\dfrac{dmg}{V}$
$q<\dfrac{mg}{v}$
$q=\dfrac{dmg}{V}$
$q=\dfrac{qvB}{E}$

questions.question: For an object to leave the Earth's gravitational field it must be projected at escape velocity. Which of the following is NOT a consideration in the definition of escape velocity?
questions.answer: Escape velocity is defined by the object just reaching infinity ($r\to\infty$) where its gravitational force (and potential energy) is zero, and $K+U=0$, so $\frac12mv^2=\frac{GMm}{r}$ with $K$ and $U$ equal in magnitude. The acceleration of the object is not a consideration, as it decreases continually (C).
options: The object reaches an infinite distance from Earth.
The Earth's gravitational force stops acting on the object.
The acceleration of the object equals the gravitational acceleration of the Earth.
The initial gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy of the object are equal in magnitude.

questions.question: All motors have a constant top speed that will be reached some time after beginning to rotate. What is the reason for the maximum top speed?
questions.answer: As the coil speeds up, the back emf (which opposes the supply emf, by Lenz's law) increases, reducing the net voltage, current and torque. At the top speed the back emf has reached its maximum value, so the net voltage across the coil (and the torque, which balances friction and load) is constant (C).
options: The back emf eventually equals the supply emf, resulting in a constant net voltage.
The supply emf gradually decreases as the back emf increases, resulting in a constant voltage in the motor.
As the motor increases in speed, the back emf increases to a maximum, resulting in a constant net voltage.
The starting resistance gradually decreases, resulting in a constant resistance that determines the maximum speed of the motor.

questions.question: Two transformers, X and Y, are shown. Which of the following shows a change made to both transformers and the resulting correct change to the output voltage?
questions.answer: $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$ is fixed by the turns ratio, so increasing $V_p$ increases $V_s$ in both (C). Changing the frequency does not change the output voltage in an ideal transformer.
options: Change: increase frequency of input AC. Result: increased voltage output in both transformers.
Change: input voltage decreased. Result: output voltage on X will increase, but decrease on Y.
Change: input voltage increased. Result: output voltage on both transformers will increase.
Change: input voltage increased. Result: output voltage on X will increase, but decrease on Y.

questions.question: The following nuclear equation shows the formation of a daughter nucleus and an unknown particle: $^{A}_{Z}X+{}^{1}_{0}n\rightarrow{}^{A-1}_{Z-2}Y+\,?$ What is the other type of particle produced?
questions.answer: Conservation of mass number: $A+1=(A-1)+m$, so the products other than Y total mass number 2. Conservation of charge: $Z=(Z-2)+q$, so total charge 2. This is two protons, $2\,{}^{1}_{1}p$ (D), each with mass number 1 and charge $+1$.

questions.question: Two satellites, A and B, orbit Earth at different altitudes (A: 629 km, B: 7629 km above the surface; Earth's radius 6371 km). Determine the ratio $T_A:T_B$.
questions.answer: $r_A=6371+629=7000$ km and $r_B=6371+7629=14000$ km. Kepler's third law: $T^2\propto r^3$, so $\dfrac{T_A}{T_B}=\left(\dfrac{r_A}{r_B}\right)^{3/2}=\left(\dfrac12\right)^{3/2}=0.354$ (C).

questions.question: The diagram shows a simple DC motor with a single rectangular coil of wire in a uniform magnetic field of strength 4.52 T. The length of side AB is 0.13 m and the length of side BC is 0.057 m. If the current flowing in the coil is 0.48 A, calculate the magnitude of the maximum torque produced by the motor.
questions.answer: $\tau_{\max}=nIAB=(1)(0.48)(0.13\times0.057)(4.52)=0.016\ \text{N m}$ (maximum when the coil's plane is parallel to the field).

questions.question: The diagram shows a simple DC motor with a single rectangular coil of wire in a uniform magnetic field. Justify one change to the motor that would increase the maximum torque.
questions.answer: $\tau_{\max}=nIAB$. Increasing the strength of the magnetic field $B$ (for example, using stronger magnets) increases the torque, because torque is directly proportional to $B$ ($\tau\propto B$). (Equally, increasing the number of turns, the current or the coil area increases the torque in proportion.)

questions.question: A red laser is shone through a double slit with slits $3.50\times10^{-5}$ m apart. The screen is 5.50 m away from the double slit. A student measures the distance between two adjacent bright bands to be 10.0 cm. Calculate the wavelength of the laser light.
questions.answer: For small angles, $\Delta y=\dfrac{\lambda L}{d}$, so $\lambda=\dfrac{d\,\Delta y}{L}=\dfrac{(3.50\times10^{-5})(0.100)}{5.50}=6.4\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}$ (640 nm). (Using $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$ with $\Delta m=1$ and $\sin\theta\approx\tan\theta=\frac{0.100}{5.50}$ gives the same result.)

questions.question: A student measures the distance between adjacent bright bands formed when a red laser is shone through a double slit onto a screen (the measured spacing is 10.0 cm). Outline a limitation of this experiment that impacts the reliability of the results.
questions.answer: The bright bands are wide and fuzzy with no clearly defined edges or centres, so deciding where each maximum is (and therefore the spacing between them) is subjective. Different measurements or different people would give different values (random error), so repeated results are not consistent, which reduces the reliability.

questions.question: An object of mass 5.25 kg moves around a point in a circle of radius 4.83 m. The object has a period of 4.10 s. Calculate the acceleration of the object.
questions.answer: $v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}=\dfrac{2\pi(4.83)}{4.10}=7.40\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. $a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r}=\dfrac{7.40^2}{4.83}=11\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ (11.3) directed towards the centre of the circle. (Acceleration is a vector, so the direction is required.)

questions.question: A planet orbits the Sun in an elliptical orbit. The shaded sectors swept out by the line from the Sun to the planet, between A and B (close to the Sun) and between C and D (far from the Sun), have equal areas. Justify whether the planet is travelling faster between A and B or between C and D.
questions.answer:
By Kepler's second law, the line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so the planet takes the same time $t$ to go from A to B as from C to D. The arc length AB is longer than arc length CD (AB is closer to the Sun, where the same swept area needs a longer arc), so $v_{AB}=\dfrac{s_{AB}}{t}>v_{CD}=\dfrac{s_{CD}}{t}$. The planet is faster between A and B.

(Equivalently, by conservation of energy: $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ is more negative closer to the Sun, so with $U+K$ constant, $K=\frac12mv^2$ and $v$ are greater between A and B.)

questions.question: Explain why a geostationary satellite in orbit around the Earth has a constant total energy.
questions.answer: A geostationary satellite stays at a constant height in a circular orbit, so its orbital radius $r$ is constant. Its orbital speed $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$ is therefore constant, so its kinetic energy $K=\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ is constant, and its gravitational potential energy $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ is constant. The total energy $U+K=-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ is therefore constant, as $G$, $M$, $m$ and $r$ are all constant.

questions.question: The graph shows information about the moons of Jupiter (radius$^3$ of orbit, in units of $10^{30}\ \text{m}^3$, against period$^2$, in units of $10^{15}\ \text{s}^2$). Use the graph to determine the mass of Jupiter.
questions.answer: Kepler's third law: $\dfrac{r^3}{T^2}=\dfrac{GM}{4\pi^2}$, so the gradient of $r^3$ against $T^2$ is $\dfrac{GM}{4\pi^2}$. Taking two widely spaced points on the line, $(0.5,\ 1.6)$ and $(3.3,\ 10.4)$: gradient $=\dfrac{(10.4-1.6)\times10^{30}}{(3.3-0.5)\times10^{15}}=3.14\times10^{15}\ \text{m}^3\text{s}^{-2}$. Then $M=\dfrac{4\pi^2\times\text{gradient}}{G}=\dfrac{4\pi^2(3.14\times10^{15})}{6.67\times10^{-11}}=1.86\times10^{27}\ \text{kg}$.

questions.question: The diagram shows three possible electron transitions in a hydrogen atom (from $n=4$, $n=3$ and $n=2$ to $n=1$). A photon of energy $1.94\times10^{-18}$ J is released from the hydrogen atom. Which electron transition from the diagram causes this energy photon?
questions.answer: $E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, so $\lambda=\dfrac{hc}{E}=\dfrac{(6.626\times10^{-34})(3.00\times10^{8})}{1.94\times10^{-18}}=1.02\times10^{-7}$ m. The final level is $n_f=1$ in all three transitions, so $\dfrac1\lambda=R\left(\dfrac1{n_f^2}-\dfrac1{n_i^2}\right)$ gives $9.76\times10^{6}=1.097\times10^{7}\left(1-\dfrac1{n_i^2}\right)$, so $\dfrac1{n_i^2}=0.111$ and $n_i^2=9.0$, $n_i=3$. The photon is emitted in the transition from $n=3$ to $n=1$.

questions.question: Models of light have changed over time as new experiments have been conducted. Outline a property of light successfully explained by Huygens but not by Newton.
questions.answer: Huygens' wave model explained diffraction and interference of light: waves spread around obstacles and through slits, and overlapping waves reinforce or cancel to form bright and dark fringes (as later shown in Young's double-slit experiment). Newton's particle (corpuscular) model, which treated light as particles travelling in straight lines, could not explain how light bends around edges or produces fringe patterns. (Refraction is another example: the wave model correctly predicts light slows in a denser medium, whereas Newton's model required it to speed up.)

questions.question: Describe a significant contribution that Maxwell made to the classical theory of electromagnetism.
questions.answer: Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism into a single theory, summarised in four equations. He showed that a changing magnetic field induces an electric field (Faraday) and, adding to Ampère's law, that a changing electric field produces a magnetic field. Together, these allow a self-sustaining electromagnetic wave, with perpendicular oscillating electric and magnetic fields travelling through space (even without a medium). He predicted that these waves travel at $c=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}\approx3\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, the measured speed of light, and so concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave. Hertz later produced and detected radio waves, confirming the prediction.

questions.question: The graphs show changes in emf generated over time by AC or DC generators. Graph 1 and Graph 3 are produced by the same type of generator. The three graphs show emf (V) against time (ms) produced by AC or DC generators. Graph 1 is a rectified (all positive) sine-wave shape with peaks of 3 V every 15 ms. Graph 2 is a sine wave alternating between +3 V and −3 V with a period of 30 ms. Graph 3 is an almost constant emf of about 4 V with small ripples at a much higher frequency. Justify which structural feature of the generators results in the different shapes of Graph 1 and Graph 3.
questions.answer: Both are DC generators, with a split-ring commutator. The generator for Graph 3 has an armature with multiple coils (for example three or more coils at different angles, each connected to its own pair of commutator segments), whereas the generator for Graph 1 has only a single coil. With several coils, when the emf of one coil falls towards zero another coil is near its maximum, so the combined output stays near its peak value, giving the smooth, almost constant emf with small ripples of Graph 3. With a single coil the emf rises to a maximum and falls to zero twice per rotation, giving the repeated humps of Graph 1.

questions.question: The graphs show changes in emf generated over time. Graph 1 and Graph 2 are produced by generators with different commutators. The three graphs show emf (V) against time (ms) produced by AC or DC generators. Graph 1 is a rectified (all positive) sine-wave shape with peaks of 3 V every 15 ms. Graph 2 is a sine wave alternating between +3 V and −3 V with a period of 30 ms. Graph 3 is an almost constant emf of about 4 V with small ripples at a much higher frequency. Explain how the different commutators result in the shapes of Graph 1 and Graph 2.
questions.answer:
Graph 2 comes from a generator with slip rings, one connected to each end of the coil. Each end of the coil is always connected to the same external contact, so as the coil rotates and the direction of the induced emf reverses every half rotation (the coil cuts the field lines in the opposite direction), the output current alternates direction. This gives a sinusoidal AC emf with positive and negative half cycles.

Graph 1 comes from a generator with a split-ring commutator: a single ring cut into two halves, each connected to one end of the coil. Each time the coil passes the vertical position where the emf is zero and about to reverse, the split gaps swap which brush each coil end touches. This reverses the connection to the external circuit at the same instant as the emf reverses, so the output always has the same polarity. The negative half-cycles are flipped to positive, giving the pulsating DC output of Graph 1, which falls to zero twice per rotation.

questions.question: Explain how the atomic model proposed by Bohr was able to overcome the significant limitation of Rutherford's 'planetary' atomic model.
questions.answer:
In Rutherford's model, electrons orbit the nucleus in circular paths held by the electrostatic force, so each electron undergoes uniform circular motion with a centripetal acceleration. According to classical electromagnetism, an accelerating charged particle emits electromagnetic radiation, so the electron would continuously lose energy, spiral into the nucleus in a very short time and emit a continuous spectrum. Atoms are observed to be stable and to emit only discrete line spectra, so the model fails.

Bohr proposed that electrons can exist in certain stable orbits called stationary states, with quantised angular momentum, in which they do not radiate energy despite their circular motion. Because an electron in a stationary state has constant energy and does not radiate, it cannot spiral into the nucleus, so the atom is stable. Electrons emit or absorb energy only when they move between stationary states, with a photon whose energy equals the difference between the two energy levels.

questions.question: Three polarising filters are set up in a line. Unpolarised light of intensity 100 units is incident on filter 1. The plane of polarisation of filter 3 is perpendicular to the plane of polarisation of filter 1. Both filter 1 and 3 are fixed in place. Filter 2 can be rotated. Identify both positions of filter 2 that will ensure that no light emerges from filter 3.
questions.answer: Let filter 2 be at angle $\theta$ to filter 1. The intensity leaving filter 3 is $I_3=I_2\cos^2(90^\circ-\theta)=I_1\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta$, which is zero when $\theta=0^\circ$ (filter 2 parallel to filter 1, same as $180^\circ$) or $\theta=90^\circ$ (filter 2 parallel to filter 3, same as $270^\circ$). In the first case, filter 3 is perpendicular to the light from filters 1 and 2; in the second, filter 2 is perpendicular to the light from filter 1 and blocks it.

questions.question: Three polarising filters are set up in a line. Unpolarised light of intensity 100 units is incident on filter 1. Determine the intensity of light transmitted from filter 2 when the plane of polarisation of filter 2 is at an angle of $30^\circ$ to that of filter 1.
questions.answer: An ideal polariser transmits half the intensity of unpolarised light, so after filter 1 the intensity is $I_1=50$ units. By Malus' law, $I_2=I_1\cos^2\theta=50\cos^2(30^\circ)=50\times0.75=37.5$ units.

questions.question: Data was collected for Stars A and B by scientists on Earth: a graph of radiation intensity against wavelength (Star A peaks at about 350 nm, Star B at about 660 nm), the stars' spectra compared with a laboratory spectrum, and a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram. Star A has a luminosity of 1, while Star B has a luminosity of $10^2$. The two stars undergo different types of fusion in the core. Compare the types of fusion occurring in the core of Star A and B and TWO other features of the stars. You must include information from all three stimulus diagrams in your response.
questions.answer:
**Surface temperature and classification (graph 1 and HR diagram).** Stars radiate as black bodies, so Wien's law $\lambda_{\max}=\dfrac bT$ gives their surface temperatures. Star A: $T_A=\dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{350\times10^{-9}}\approx8300\ \text{K}$; Star B: $T_B=\dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{662.5\times10^{-9}}\approx4400\ \text{K}$. Plotting each star on the HR diagram using temperature and luminosity: Star A (about 8300 K, luminosity 1) lies on the main sequence, in the hot, white (A/F) region. Star B (about 4400 K, luminosity $10^2$) lies in the red giant region, so it is a cool, red-orange (K-type), very large star that has left the main sequence.

**Type of fusion.** Star A is a main-sequence star fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, here by the proton–proton chain, which has a low enough core temperature for this (net: $4\,{}^{1}_{1}\text{H}\rightarrow{}^{4}_{2}\text{He}+2e^{+}+2\nu+\text{energy}$). (More massive, hotter main-sequence stars fuse hydrogen to helium by the CNO cycle instead, which needs a higher core temperature; CNO also does not produce more than helium.) Star B is a red giant, which has finished fusing hydrogen in its core. Post-main-sequence fusion occurs: hydrogen fuses in a shell around an inert helium core, which contracts and heats until helium fuses to carbon and oxygen (triple-alpha process), and in more massive stars progressively heavier elements (up to iron) fuse in shells, layered around the core as each fuel runs out.

**Translational velocity (spectra).** The stars' absorption lines are compared with the laboratory spectrum of the same element, whose lines are at known wavelengths. Star A's lines are shifted only slightly towards the red end, while Star B's lines are shifted more towards the red end. By the Doppler effect, red-shift shows that both stars are moving away from Earth, with Star B moving away faster (greater translational velocity). Because $\dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}=\dfrac vc$, the larger shift gives the larger recession speed.

questions.question: A charged particle $q_1$ is projected horizontally into a vertical electric field $E_1$ with an initial velocity $u_1$. A particle $q_2$ of identical charge and mass is projected horizontally into a different electric field $E_2$ with an initial velocity of $u_2$. The physical setup of the two parallel plates, including their length and the distance between the plates, is identical. It is known that $u_1>u_2$ and $E_2>E_1$, and that the particles will hit the bottom plates in both electric fields before leaving the field. A student predicted that particle $q_1$ will travel further than particle $q_2$ before hitting the bottom plate. Analyse the accuracy of the prediction made by the student.
questions.answer:
The particle moves like a projectile: constant horizontal velocity and constant vertical acceleration $a=\dfrac{F}{m}=\dfrac{qE}{m}$. Since $q$ and $m$ are the same, $a\propto E$, so $a_2>a_1$.

Vertical motion (starting with zero vertical velocity): $s_y=\tfrac12at^2$, so $t=\sqrt{\dfrac{2s_y}{a}}$, and as the plate separation $s_y$ is the same, $t\propto\dfrac1{\sqrt a}$. Since $a_2>a_1$, $t_2<t_1$.

Horizontal motion: no horizontal force, so the horizontal distance (range) is $R=ut$. Since $u_1>u_2$ and $t_1>t_2$, $R_1=u_1t_1>R_2=u_2t_2$.

So particle $q_1$ travels further than $q_2$ before hitting the bottom plate, and the student's prediction is accurate.

questions.question: Hubble's observations provided evidence that the universe is expanding. Describe the observations that led Hubble to conclude that the universe was expanding.
questions.answer: Hubble measured the distances to galaxies (using Cepheid variable stars as standard candles, from their apparent and absolute magnitudes) and measured their velocities from the Doppler shift of the spectral lines in their light compared with laboratory spectra. He observed that the spectral lines of almost all galaxies were shifted towards longer wavelengths (red-shifted), meaning that they are moving away from us, and that the more distant the galaxy, the greater its red-shift and recession speed ($v\propto d$, $v=H_0d$). This pattern, in which everything moves away from everything else faster with distance, is explained by the expansion (stretching) of space itself, which stretches the wavelengths of light.

questions.question: Hubble's observations provided evidence that the universe is expanding. Sketch a graph of the data collected during Hubble's observations and outline how it allows the age of the universe to be estimated.
questions.answer:
The graph of recession velocity $v$ (vertical axis) against distance $d$ (horizontal axis) is a straight line through the origin, with gradient the Hubble constant $H_0$ ($v=H_0d$), as shown.

If the galaxies have always moved at constant speed, the time since they were together at the same point (the Big Bang) is $t=\dfrac dv=\dfrac1{H_0}$, which is the inverse of the gradient. This gives an estimate of the age of the universe (about 14 billion years for $H_0\approx70\ \text{km s}^{-1}\text{Mpc}^{-1}$).

questions.question: Explain how the equations $K_{\max}=hf-\phi$ (proposed by Einstein in the analysis of the photoelectric effect) and $\dfrac1\lambda=R\left(\dfrac1{n_f^2}-\dfrac1{n_i^2}\right)$ (used by Bohr for the analysis of emission spectra for hydrogen) are BOTH related to quantised energy and are BOTH consistent with the law of conservation of energy.
questions.answer:
**Photoelectric effect: quantised energy.** Einstein proposed that light consists of photons, each carrying a discrete quantum of energy $E=hf$ (the idea of quantised energy introduced by Planck). In $K_{\max}=hf-\phi$, the term $hf$ is the energy of a single photon, which is absorbed by a single electron as a whole, and the work function $\phi$ is the minimum energy to remove an electron from the metal. Energy transfers only occur in whole photons, so emission occurs only if $hf\ge\phi$ (the threshold frequency).

**Photoelectric effect: conservation of energy.** Rearranged, $hf=K_{\max}+\phi$: the energy input (the photon's energy) equals the energy output (the work done to free the electron plus the electron's maximum kinetic energy). No energy is lost: $E_{in}=E_{out}$.

**Hydrogen emission spectra: quantised energy.** Bohr proposed that electrons in hydrogen can only exist in discrete energy levels (stationary states) with energies proportional to $-\dfrac1{n^2}$. In the equation, $n_i$ and $n_f$ are whole numbers labelling these quantised levels, and $\dfrac1\lambda\propto\dfrac{E}{hc}$ is proportional to the energy of the emitted photon ($E=hf=\dfrac{hc}\lambda$), so only certain photon energies (spectral lines of particular wavelengths) are possible, rather than a continuous spectrum.

**Hydrogen emission spectra: conservation of energy.** The bracket $\left(\dfrac1{n_f^2}-\dfrac1{n_i^2}\right)$ is proportional to the energy lost by the electron when it falls from level $n_i$ to level $n_f$, and $\dfrac1\lambda$ is proportional to the energy of the emitted photon. The equation therefore equates the energy released by the electron to the energy of the photon emitted ($E_i-E_f=hf$), so energy is conserved.

questions.question: Two oppositely charged parallel plates are arranged vertically 8.5 cm apart with 15 000 V between them. A ball of mass 2.7 g and carrying a charge of +69 nC is suspended by a massless string from the top of the positive plate, as shown, and hangs in equilibrium. Calculate the magnitude of the tension in the string. Use $g=9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.
questions.answer: Three forces act on the ball: weight $F_g=mg=(2.7\times10^{-3})(9.8)=2.65\times10^{-2}$ N (down), electric force $F_E=qE=\dfrac{qV}{d}=\dfrac{(69\times10^{-9})(15000)}{0.085}=1.22\times10^{-2}$ N (horizontal, towards the negative plate), and tension $T$ along the string. The ball is in equilibrium, so the tension balances the vector sum of the other two forces: $T=\sqrt{F_g^2+F_E^2}=\sqrt{(2.65\times10^{-2})^2+(1.22\times10^{-2})^2}=2.9\times10^{-2}$ N.

questions.question: A ball carrying a positive charge is suspended by a massless string from the top of the positive one of two oppositely charged vertical parallel plates. Sketch on the diagram the path of the ball if the string was to break. Justify your predicted path. Calculations are not required.
questions.answer: When the string breaks, the ball is at rest and the only forces are its weight (constant, vertically down) and the electric force (constant, horizontal towards the negative plate, as the field between the plates is uniform). The resultant force is constant and is the same as the tension in magnitude but opposite in direction (the equilibrium condition before the string broke), so the ball accelerates uniformly from rest in the direction of that constant resultant force. Since the initial velocity is zero and the acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction, the ball moves in a straight line, down and towards the negative plate, at $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{F_E}{F_g}\approx25^\circ$ from the vertical (along the line of the former string, extended away from the point of suspension), until it hits the negative plate.

questions.question: Two solenoids are positioned close to each other. Solenoid A is connected to a power source. Solenoid B is connected to a cathode ray oscilloscope (CRO) that outputs data showing emf generated over a period of time. An experiment investigates how the CRO output from Solenoid B changes when the current in Solenoid A is changed. Test 1: direct current (DC) of magnitude 1.5 A. Test 2: alternating current (AC) of magnitude 3.0 A. Sketch and explain the observed CRO output (emf against time) from Solenoid B for Test 1 and Test 2.
questions.answer:
**Test 1 (steady DC).** The steady current of 1.5 A in Solenoid A produces a constant magnetic field, so the flux linking Solenoid B is constant. By Faraday's law, $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=0$, so the CRO shows a flat line at zero emf (apart from a brief pulse when the current is switched on or off).

**Test 2 (AC).** The alternating current changes continuously in magnitude and direction, sinusoidally, so the magnetic field of Solenoid A and the flux through Solenoid B change continuously. The induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of flux, which is greatest when the current is changing most rapidly (at zero current) and zero when the current is at a maximum or minimum. The emf in Solenoid B is therefore also sinusoidal (alternating) with the same frequency as the current (a quarter cycle out of phase with it). Its amplitude is larger than any emf in Test 1 (the flux changes at a greater rate with the larger 3.0 A current).
